<reason>PRO built a clear, stable frame from the opening (chosen premium vs. extracted premium; the "competitor" is the restaurant whose food is already in the cart) and defended it consistently. CON's strongest opening lines — "compelled cross-promotion of a rival" and the slippery slope — were largely dismantled by PRO's same-seller reading, which the motion's own "direct-order" language supports; CON's pressure question on this got a direct answer and CON's "narrowing" charge did not land since PRO's position was stable from [A2.5]. CON's workability/data points were partly answered (apps already publish unaudited restaurant-typed prices; materiality means silence when uncertain). CON's best material came late: the feedback-loop distinction on liability [B4.3] was genuinely sharp and PRO's closing waved it away rather than engaging it, and the loss-aversion answer to PRO's dichotomy [B4.1] was a real response. But to a third-party reader, CON's core survival argument amounts to "showing customers an accurate comparison will cause them to decline to pay," which PRO effectively turned into a confession in [A5.2]-[A5.5]. CON's "behavioral economics is unambiguous" was somewhat overconfident, and the fee-relocation mechanism still presupposes that orders lost to true information were legitimately the app's. Both sides had clipped turns, roughly offsetting. PRO made the decisive choice clearer and won the weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's dichotomy in [A3.1]/[A4.5] — if the premium is genuine value no orders are lost, and if orders are lost they were sustained by ignorance — forced CON into the loss-aversion defense in [B4.1], which PRO then reframed in closing as CON conceding that the comparison is true and customers will bail on seeing it. CON's feedback-loop answer [B4.3] was the sharpest single counter but arrived too late to be fully contested.</best_rebuttal>
